'''John Rowland Mallard''' [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] [[Royal Society of Edinburgh|FRSE]] [[FREng]] (14 January 1927<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=hm9qAAAAMAAJ&q=john+rowland+mallard+1927 International Who's Who in Medicine, p. 300]</ref> – 25 February 2021)<ref>{{Cite web |author=Georgina Ferry |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/mar/12/john-mallard-obituary |title=John Mallard obituary |website=[[TheGuardian.com]] |date=12 March 2021 |access-date=2021-06-14}}</ref> was an English physicist and [[professor]] of [[Medical Physics]] at the [[University of Aberdeen]] from 1965 until his retirement in 1992. He was known for setting up and leading the team that developed the first [[magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI) full body scanner and, in particular, [[positron emission tomography]] (PET). He was born in [[Kingsthorpe]], [[Northampton]], England.<ref>{{cite news|last=Duggan|first=Jack|title=Tributes paid to 'pioneering' Northampton-born physicist responsible for breakthroughs in medical imaging|url=https://www.northamptonchron.co.uk/news/people/tributes-paid-to-pioneering-northampton-born-physicist-responsible-for-breakthroughs-in-medical-imaging-3150368|work=Northampton Chronicle and Echo|location=Northampton|access-date=1 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.northamptonboroughcouncil.com/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=242&MId=7966|title=Agenda for Council on Monday, 25 January 2016, 6:30 pm|first=Northampton Borough|last=Council|date=25 January 2016|website=www.northamptonboroughcouncil.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |author=David J. Lurie |author2=Peter F. Sharp  |journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine |title=In memoriam: John R. Mallard (1927-2021) |date= 6 June 2021 |volume=86 |issue=4 |pages=1815–1817 |doi=10.1002/mrm.28838 |pmid=34096094 |quote=John Mallard (Figure 1) passed away on February 25, 2021.|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Career==
Mallard completed his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] research into magnetic properties of [[uranium]] at [[University of Nottingham|University College, Nottingham]] under Professor [[Leslie Fleetwood Bates]] in 1947.<ref>{{cite journal|jstor=36203|doi=10.1098/rspb.1986.0001|bibcode=1986RSPSB.226..391M|title=The Wellcome Foundation Lecture, 1984 - Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging in medicine: Medical and biological applications and problems|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B. Biological Sciences|year=1986|volume=226|issue=1245|pages=391–419|last1=Mallard|first1=J. R.|pmid=2869495|s2cid=20542289}}</ref><ref name=bmb/>

Mallard worked as Assistant Physicist with the Liverpool Radium Institute where he completed his training in hospital physics.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://calm.abdn.ac.uk/archives/Record.aspx?src=CalmView.Catalog&id=AMCS%2F4%2F6|title=Record AMCS - Records of the Aberdeen Medico-Chirurgical Society|publisher=The University of Aberdeen|access-date=28 February 2021}}</ref> He joined [[Hammersmith Hospital]] and Post Graduate Medical School in 1953,<ref name=bmb>{{cite journal|doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.bmb.a071974|title=Notes on Contributors|journal=British Medical Bulletin|year=1984|volume=40|issue=2|pages=202–204}}</ref> and in 1959 Mallard developed the first whole-body isotope scanner (homemade) in the UK, used for detecting a brain tumour, with C.&nbsp;J. Peachey.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1007/s00259-019-04413-5|title=The 70th anniversary of automated radionuclide imaging|year=2019|last1=McCready|first1=V. Ralph|journal=European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging|volume=46|issue=12|pages=2414–2417|pmid=31420697|doi-access=free}}</ref> Mallard published his theories on electron spin resonance and cancer in the journal [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] in 1964 but they went largely unnoticed.<ref name=uoa/> In 1965 he was appointed the first chair of Medical Physics at the [[University of Aberdeen]], predicting at his first lecture that positron emission tomography (PET) would become one of the most important tools for diagnosis and studying of diseases.<ref name=uoa/> Mallard brought to Scotland its first PET scanner, leading a national fundraising campaign and agreeing to bring a second-hand research machine from London. The scanner was located in a facility next to [[Woodend Hospital]], which has been since replaced by the John Mallard PET Centre at the [[Aberdeen Royal Infirmary]].<ref name=uoa/>

In the 1970s, Mallard set up and led a team, which included James Hutchison and Dr Bill Edelstein,<ref name=scm>{{cite web|url=https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/ap28066/mallard-john-r|title=Mallard, John R 1927|publisher=The Science Museum|access-date=1 March 2021}}</ref> to build the first MRI full body scanner. The scanner was first used on 28 August 1980,<ref name=scm/> to scan a terminal cancer patient,<ref name=bbc/> before being replaced in 1983.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ghat-art.org.uk/mark-1-the-worlds-first-whole-body-mri-scanner/|title=Mark-1 The world's first whole-body MRI Scanner|publisher=Grampian Hospital'a Art Trust|access-date=28 February 2021}}</ref> During the 1980s, Mallard discovered "spin warp imaging", a technique that could produce three-dimensional images unaffected by the movement of patients.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://autm.net/about-tech-transfer/better-world-project/bwp-stories/mri-scanners|title=Super Vision: MRI Scanners Replace the Need for Riskier Surgical Procedures|publisher=University of Nottingham|access-date=28 February 2021}}</ref> During the 1980s, there was a discussion on where MRI scanners should be based because radiologists were used to images not numbers, Mallard was quoted as saying:

"The human body is extremely complex. When, in addition, we first attempt to image a new property such as proton magnetic resonance, there is bound to be difficulty in interpreting the results... With this in mind, we have carried out a biological back-up program of T1 measurement on normal and pathological tissues to ease the problem of image interpretation and to find pointers toward the most fruitful fields for the application of NMR imaging" <ref name=kelly>{{cite journal |doi=10.1080/09505430600639322|title=From numbers to pictures: The development of magnetic resonance imaging and the visual turn in medicine|year=2006|last1=Joyce|first1=Kelly A.|journal=Science as Culture|volume=15|pages=1–22|s2cid=42503421}}</ref>

Later in the 1980s, when imaging became standard on scanners, Mallard's team had originally developed the images in colour but had to transfer them into greyscale as radiologists were not used to colour.<ref name=kelly/> In the early 80s Mallard appointed David Lurie as postdoctoral researcher within the MRI team, suggesting he work on free radical imaging.<ref name=uoa/>

Mallard retired from the [[University of Aberdeen]] in 1992.<ref name=uoa/> Mallard was founder Secretary General of the International Organization for Medical Physics and went on to become its president. He was also Founder President of the International Union of Physical and Engineering Sciences in Medicine.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ipem.ac.uk/NewsExternalAffairs/LatestNews/TabId/366/ArtMID/1595/ArticleID/555/Professor-John-Mallard-OBE-FRSE.aspx|title=PROFESSOR JOHN MALLARD OBE FRSE|publisher=Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine|access-date=28 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.iomp.org/obituary-prof-john-mallard/|title=Obituary: Prof. John Mallard|date=26 February 2021 |publisher=International Organization for Medical Physics|access-date=28 February 2021}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
In 1972 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rse.org.uk/fellow/john-mallard/|title=Professor John Rowland Mallard OBE FREng FRSE |publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|access-date=6 March 2018|language=en-GB}}</ref> and a [[Fellow]] of the [[Royal Academy of Engineering]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows|title=List of Fellows|access-date=21 October 2014|archive-date=8 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160608094405/http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows}}</ref> in 1993. In 1998, the John Mallard Scottish PET Centre was opened in [[Aberdeen Royal Infirmary]] by the [[List of Scottish Executive ministerial teams|Minister for Health]], [[Sam Galbraith]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scotland.gov.uk/news/releas98_2/pr1908.htm|title=Galbraith hails new scanning centre in Scotland|date=23 September 1998|publisher=Scottish Office}}</ref> He was honoured with the [[Freedom of the City of Aberdeen]] in 2004.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iop.org/activity/groups/subject/med/News/page_8204.html|title=Professor John Mallard to receive Freedom of the City of Aberdeen|publisher=Institute of Physics|date=14 August 2004}}</ref> In 2004 the [[Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine]] established a lecture in his name, to be given annually at the United Kingdom Radiological Congress.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ipem.ac.uk/ConferencesEvents/EponymousLectures/JohnMallardLecture.aspx|title=John Mallard Lecture|publisher=Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> Mallard honours also include the Royal Society Wellcome Prize and gold medal, the George von Hevesy Memorial Lecture Medal, the Royal Medal of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, the Landau Memorial Plaque of the American Association of Physicists in Medicine, and the Academic Enterprise Competition Prize of the British Technology Group.<ref name=uoa>{{cite web|url=https://www.abdn.ac.uk/news/14707/|title=Head of pioneering MRI team passes away|publisher=University of Aberdeen|access-date=28 February 2021}}</ref>

==Death==
Mallard died, at the age of 94, on 25 February 2021.<ref name=bbc>{{Cite news|title=Aberdeen physicist behind first full-body MRI scanner dies|publisher=[[BBC News]]|date=26 February 2021|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-scotland-north-east-orkney-shetland-56217687|access-date=26 February 2021|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Walker|first=David|title=John Mallard: Aberdeen professor who helped create first full-body MRI scan dies at 94|url=https://www.eveningexpress.co.uk/fp/news/local/john-mallard-aberdeen-professor-who-helped-create-first-full-body-mri-scan-dies-at-94/|date=26 February 2021|access-date=26 February 2021|work=[[Evening Express (Scotland)|Evening Express]]|language=en-GB|archive-date=27 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227130417/https://www.eveningexpress.co.uk/fp/news/local/john-mallard-aberdeen-professor-who-helped-create-first-full-body-mri-scan-dies-at-94/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Professor John Mallard OBE FRSE|url=https://www.ipem.ac.uk/news/professor-john-mallard-obe-frse/|access-date=13 November 2022|publisher=[[Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine]]|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/mar/12/john-mallard-obituary|title=John Mallard obituary: Medical physicist who pioneered body scanning as a way to diagnose disease|first=Georgina|last=Ferry|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=12 March 2021|access-date=13 November 2022}}</ref>
